description:
Qiqumaniq means permafrost in Inuvialuktun. We are turning NISAR L-band radar and historical RADARSAT-1 data into an open-source web map showing how permafrost ground sinks and heaves along the Inuvik–Tuktoyaktuk corridor (NWT), and how far the coast near Tuktoyaktuk has retreated. The science spec is written; the data pipeline is being built now.

Looking for teammates in SAR/InSAR, Python geospatial (xarray, rasterio), web mapping (MapLibre/Leaflet, JS), or science storytelling/video.
summary:
Arctic Breathing Ground (Qiqumaniq) is an open-source web app. It turns NISAR L-band radar data into plain answers about ground on permafrost. Its core question is: how much did the ground under this place move this season, and how much can I trust that number?

A user selects or registers a place: a point, a line or an area. The app gives the ground motion relative to the nearby ground, the date when the ground surface froze, and the shoreline change since 2003. Each result shows its confidence, its source and its limits. Where the radar has no reliable signal, the app says so. Two lenses show the same data: Community (plain words) and Engineer (numbers, uncertainty, method and data download).

The sample places are in the Inuvik–Tuktoyaktuk corridor, Northwest Territories: the highway, two airports and the Tuktoyaktuk shoreline. The shoreline moved back a median of 23.8 m from 2003 to 2026. The ground surface froze between 11 October and 4 November 2026. We tested the results against criteria that we set before we saw them: 10 pass, 5 fail, 1 not tested.

The app is a screening tool: it shows where to look first. It does not predict failures.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ground on ice-rich permafrost sinks in summer and rises in winter. Warming melts ground ice, and the ground ends each year a little lower. Roads, airstrips and coasts in the North move a few centimetres each year, and people do not see it until something breaks. Radar satellites measure this motion, but the data is hard to read without radar training.

Arctic Breathing Ground (Qiqumaniq) is a web app. A user selects or registers a place (a point, a line or an area). The user can draw the place, load a GeoJSON file or paste coordinates. The app gives three views:

- Ground motion: the motion of the place relative to the ground 300 m to 1 km around it, in the 2026 thaw season.

- Freeze and thaw: the date when the radar saw the ground surface freeze.

- Then and now: shoreline change from 2003 (RADARSAT-1) to 2026 (NISAR), and a qualitative comparison with 2017 airborne radar (NASA ABoVE).

Each result has one plain sentence, one confidence word, one limit sentence and its source. The Community lens uses plain words. The Engineer lens shows the numbers, the uncertainty, the method and a data download.

HOW IT WORKS

- Ground motion: we stack NISAR L2 GUNW (provisional) interferograms from 25 June to 11 October 2026. The ionosphere adds stripes up to 10 cm, and the thaw signal is only 1 cm to 5 cm. Thus we do not show the full map as measured motion. We compare each place with the ground around it, which removes most of the stripes. A permutation test (the highway shape moved to 2000 random places) gives the significance.

- Freeze-up: we read NISAR L2 GCOV backscatter on 11 dates from 25 June to 4 November 2026. A drop of 2 dB or more from the summer level marks freeze-up.

- Shoreline: we find the land and water edge on a RADARSAT-1 image (23 June 2003) and a NISAR image (24 August 2026). We measure the change on 86 transects, 250 m apart (USGS DSAS method).

- A backend makes layer products for an area and a period. A registered place uses only these products, so results come in seconds. Each run records its inputs and their SHA-256 values.

RESULTS ON THE SAMPLE PLACES

- Tuktoyaktuk shoreline: median retreat 23.8 m from 2003 to 2026 (1.03 m per year), uncertainty ±21.4 m per transect. This is in the published range of 1 m to 2 m per year.

- Inuvik–Tuktoyaktuk Highway: about 0.4 to 0.5 cm difference from the nearby tundra (p = 0.024). Confidence is low: one season, one satellite, and a Sentinel-1 cross-check did not confirm it. It is a hypothesis for engineers, not a measurement of the road surface.

- Freeze-up along the highway: 11 October to 4 November 2026 at 14 sites. This is up to about 3 weeks after the air temperature went below 0 °C, because the radar sees the ground freeze, not the air.

- Ibyuk Pingo (live test): the app returned results in 7 seconds. For ground motion it said "no data here" (0 valid radar pixels) and gave the reason.

VALIDATION

We wrote a validation plan before we saw the results, and we did not change the criteria after. Result: 10 pass, 5 fail, 1 not tested. The shoreline agrees with its published reference. Ground motion and freeze-up do not agree with their references (Sentinel-1, weather-station air temperature and SMAP), and the app says so. We estimate the system at TRL 4 and the shoreline method at TRL 5.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- People in Inuvik and Tuktoyaktuk can see if the ground under their road, homes and coast moves.

- Engineers can choose which highway segments or airstrips need field work first.

- Planners and councils get evidence with its confidence and its limits.

The product starts in the Inuvik–Tuktoyaktuk corridor. A new region needs new layer products, not a change to the app.

LIMITS

NISAR products are provisional. We have one season, so we cannot separate seasonal from permanent subsidence. The pixel spacing is 80 m, so the app shows the ground around a structure, not the structure. InSAR gives motion relative to a reference, not absolute motion. We do not state the direction of motion, because the NISAR phase sign is not confirmed. The user groups are proto-personas from published sources; we did not interview users yet. The app is not a source of engineering design data.

TOOLS

Python (numpy, scipy, rasterio, h5py, scikit-image, shapely, pyproj, asf_search, pystac), FastAPI, Celery, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, Docker Compose, Next.js and React, MapLibre GL JS, geotiff.js, OpenTelemetry and reveal.js. Code licence: Apache-2.0. Data layers: CC BY 4.0. Files with OpenStreetMap data: ODbL 1.0.

INUVIALUKTUN TERMS

Inuvialuktun terms — qiqumaniq (permafrost; all three dialects), nunakput auktualihuni (Uummarmiutun; literally "our land is thawing") and nunam sinaa situyuaq (Sallirmiutun; coastal erosion) — are from the Inuvialuktun Climate Change, Energy and Science Glossary, © 2025 Inuvialuit Regional Corporation, used for non-commercial educational purposes with acknowledgement.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) and Gemini Argo (Google) for brainstorming and for the concept note. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help with research, plans, documents, code and the demo slides. We used Google Gemini to make our team image. The image has a visible watermark. A team member examined all SI output. All scientific results come from the NISAR, RADARSAT-1 and other cited data. They do not come from an SI model. No SI output uses NASA branding.
